ta-l1d8q2-d1e97.summary: Transitional paragraph opening the inquiry into the measure of divine being, eternity, in three articles: what eternity is, to whom it belongs, and whether verbs of different tenses can be predicated of the eternal.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e109.summary: Presents Boethius's definition of eternity, 'the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of interminable life' (Consolation 5), and a first objection: 'interminable' expresses a negation, and negation does not make anything certain, so it should not be in a definition.
claims: Negations do not define.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e115.summary: Second objection. The first measure corresponds to the first thing measured, and the first measured is being. Eternity, the first measure, should be defined by being, not life.
claims: The first measure should be defined by the first measured, being.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e118.summary: Third objection. The simple has no measure; rather the simplest measures everything else (the Philosopher). Divine life is simplest, so nothing measures it, and eternity, which implies measure, does not apply.
claims: The simplest is the measure of others and is not itself measured.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e122.summary: Fourth objection. 'Whole' is said with respect to parts, and the parts of a duration are not simultaneous; two durations cannot coexist unless one includes the other (Augustine). So 'whole' and 'simultaneous' seem contradictory.
claims: The parts of a duration are not simultaneous.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e128.summary: Fifth objection. 'Whole' already includes perfection, so 'perfect' is redundant.
claims: 'Whole' implies perfection.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e134.summary: Sixth objection. Eternity is a duration, but 'possession' says nothing about duration, so it should not stand in the definition as its genus, which must say what the defined thing is.
claims: The genus in a definition must say what the thing is.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e140.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Eternity' means being outside limits (termini), and being can be limited in three ways. (1) In its whole duration, by beginning and end. (2) In the parts of its duration, each limited by what precedes and follows, as in motion. (3) By the supposit in which it is received: being is received according to the receiver's mode and so limited, like any form that is common of itself, and only divine being is unlimited in this way, since it is received in nothing distinct from it. 'Interminable life' excludes the first limit and separates the eternal from what is generated and corrupted. 'Whole and simultaneous' excludes the second, succession of parts, and separates eternity from motion and time even if these had always been. 'Perfect' excludes the third and separates eternal being from the being of immobile created things, such as spiritual creatures, whose being is participated.
claims: Being can be limited by beginning and end, by succession of parts, or by reception in a subject.
'Interminable' excludes beginning and end; 'whole and simultaneous' excludes succession; 'perfect' excludes limitation by a receiver.
Only divine being is not received in anything distinct from it.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e152.summary: Reply to the first objection. Simple, and above all divine, things are best manifested by remotion (Dionysius), since the intellect cannot fully comprehend their being and is led by negations to know them somehow; a point too is defined by negation. Also, eternity contains a negation, since it is unity, and unity is undividedness, which cannot be defined without negation.
claims: Simple and divine things are best made known by negation.
Eternity, as a kind of unity, includes negation in its definition.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e155.summary: Reply to the second objection. 'Life' is taken broadly here for all being, as Augustine says every change in a creature is a kind of death. Alternatively, in the one who alone has eternity, being and living are wholly the same, so Boethius made eternity the measure of life by reason of the act in which eternity lies.
claims: In God being and living are identical.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e159.summary: Reply to the third objection. Living and being are said by way of act, and every act has its own measure, so eternity must be understood to belong to divine being and life as their measure, though it is not really other than divine being. Since living has more the character of act than being, Boethius perhaps defined eternity by life rather than by being.
claims: Eternity is understood as the measure of divine being, though really identical with it.
Living has more the character of act than being.
concepts: identity of eternity and divine esse

ta-l1d8q2-d1e162.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Successive things have a twofold imperfection: division, and succession, since one part does not exist with another and they have being only in part. To exclude all imperfection from divine being, it must be understood as perfect without division of parts, which 'whole' expresses, since it does not imply parts here, and without succession, which 'simultaneous' expresses.
claims: 'Whole' excludes division of parts and 'simultaneous' excludes succession.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e165.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. Being can be imperfect in two ways. It can lack part of its due duration, as the life of one who dies in childhood is imperfect, which 'whole' removes. Or it can be imperfect in its mode of having, as every creature's being is, which 'perfect' removes. So 'perfect' is not redundant.
claims: 'Whole' removes imperfection of duration; 'perfect' removes imperfection in the mode of having being.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e168.summary: Reply to the sixth objection. 'Duration' by its very name implies a kind of extension, which must not be understood in divine being. So Boethius used 'possession' metaphorically to signify the repose of divine being: we possess what we hold quietly and fully, and God is said to possess his life because no disquiet troubles him.
claims: Boethius uses 'possession' rather than 'duration' to exclude extension and signify the repose of divine being.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e180.summary: First argument that eternity does not belong to God alone. Eternity is not nobler than goodness, which is communicated to creatures, so eternity can be communicated too.
claims: Goodness is communicated to creatures.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e183.summary: Second argument from Daniel 12:3: those who instruct many in justice will shine like stars for perpetual eternities. Several eternities do not belong to one eternal being, so there are several eternals.
claims: Scripture speaks of plural eternities.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e189.summary: Third argument from Psalm 75:5, 'from the eternal mountains': mountains are creatures, so creatures are eternal.
claims: Scripture calls mountains eternal.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e196.summary: Fourth argument: the fire of hell is called eternal (Matt. 25:41).
claims: Hell's fire is called eternal.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e202.summary: Fifth argument. The Philosopher says everything necessary is eternal, and many things are necessary; Augustine says truth is eternal.
claims: Everything necessary is eternal.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e205.summary: Sed contra. The eternal is unlimited being, and only God is such.
claims: Only God is unlimited being.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e208.summary: Thomas's determination. By the definition, eternity belongs simply and absolutely, in its full character, only to God. Things are called eternal by participation insofar as they share in eternity's interminability, and what shares in it not at all, the temporal with beginning and end, is in no way eternal. Some things share the absence of an end, as hell's fire does; whether something can lack a beginning is left for Book II. Spiritual creatures share the absence of succession, since their being is whole at once. The interminability that excludes all imperfection is communicated to no creature, since none is simply perfect, though creatures can be perfect according to their nature, as the blessed angels and humans have all their nature can hold. The blessed angels therefore participate eternity more than angels considered in their natural endowments alone. This yields the difference between eternity, aevum, and time. What has a potency that does not receive its whole act at once is measured by time, being limited both in its mode of participation and in its parts of duration. What has a potency distinct from act but receiving the whole act at once is measured by aevum, limited only by being received in another. What has no potency distinct from its being is measured by eternity, being unlimited in every way. So aevum is a participated eternity.
claims: Eternity belongs properly to God alone; creatures are eternal only by participation.
Hell's fire shares endlessness; spiritual creatures share the absence of succession; none shares the absence of all limitation.
Time measures potency not receiving its act all at once; aevum measures potency receiving its whole act at once; eternity measures being without potency.
Aevum is a participated eternity.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e211.summary: Reply to the first argument. Divine goodness is communicable, but not in the highest mode, as it is in God; supreme goodness is not communicated. Eternity implies being in the highest mode found in God, so it is not communicated, though being taken absolutely is communicated, as goodness is.
claims: Supreme goodness and eternity, as the highest mode of being, are not communicated.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e214.summary: Reply to the second argument. Daniel speaks of the eternities participated by the blessed, which are many according to the many blessed.
claims: The plural eternities are participated eternities of the blessed.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e218.summary: Reply to the third argument. The 'eternal mountains' can be the angels, eternal by participation, or literally bodily mountains, called eternal for their long duration.
claims: Mountains are called eternal figuratively, as angels, or by long duration.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e221.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Hell's fire is called eternal because it shares one condition of eternity, having no end.
claims: Hell's fire is eternal only in being endless.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e224.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Necessary things are eternal only in the divine mind, as the truths of propositions were in God from eternity and not otherwise, unless creatures were posited as eternal, as the philosophers held.
claims: Necessary truths are eternal only in the divine mind.
concepts: eternal truths in the divine mind

ta-l1d8q2-d1e236.summary: First objection that temporal verbs cannot be said of God. Each thing has its proper measure, time is the proper measure of motion, and there is no motion in God.
claims: Time is the measure of motion.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e239.summary: Second objection. Whatever implies a bodily condition is said of God metaphorically, and time is a condition following bodies, since it follows motion and motion follows magnitude. So temporal verbs are said of God only metaphorically.
claims: Time is a bodily condition following motion and magnitude.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e242.summary: Third objection, that only the present should be said of God. Eternity lacks succession, and only the present excludes succession; past and future are said relative to the present in an order of succession.
claims: Only the present tense excludes succession.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e246.summary: Fourth objection, that the past should be said most. Divine being is perfect, and the past tense most suggests perfection.
claims: The past tense signifies completion.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e249.summary: Fifth objection, that the imperfect past should be said most. John speaks most loftily of God in his prologue and uses the imperfect tense: 'In the beginning was (erat) the Word'.
claims: John uses the imperfect tense for divine eternity.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e255.summary: Sixth objection, that the future should be said most. Divine being is furthest from failing, and the future is most remote from failing.
claims: The future is furthest from ceasing.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e258.summary: Thomas's determination. A statement can be made about something only as it is known, and every knower knows according to its own mode (Boethius). Since our reason, in this life, naturally grasps with time, its knowledge arising from sensible things in time, it can form statements only with tensed verbs. So in speaking of God it must use temporal verbs, though it understands him to be above time. These statements are not false. As Dionysius says, divine being pre-contains as cause all being with respect to its perfection, so we predicate verbs of all tenses of God, because he is absent from no time and has whatever is perfect in all times.
claims: We must speak of God with tensed verbs because our knowledge arises from temporal things.
Tensed statements about God are true, because God is present to all times and contains the perfection of each.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e261.summary: Reply to the first objection. When temporal verbs are said of God, our intellect attributes to him not what is imperfect in each time but what is perfect in all. Eternity includes in a simple way all the perfection that is divided among times, since time imitates the perfection of eternity as far as it can.
claims: Eternity contains simply the perfection divided among the times.
Time imitates eternity.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e264.summary: Reply to the second objection. A word can imply a bodily condition either in what it principally signifies, in which case it is said of God only symbolically (lion, lamb, anger), or only in its mode of signifying, in which case it is said of God properly, though it does not represent him perfectly. Otherwise all divine names would be symbolic, since their mode of signifying follows their use of creatures. 'Was' and 'will be' are of the latter kind: they signify essence by way of act and co-signify time.
claims: Names implying bodily conditions in their signified content are symbolic; those implying them only in their mode of signifying are proper.
Tensed verbs signify essence by way of act and only co-signify time.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e268.summary: Reply to the third objection. Insofar as the present implies no succession and includes nothing of non-being, it fits God most properly. Yet verbs of the other tenses are said of God according to what is perfect in them, not by reason of succession or any defect.
claims: The present tense fits God most properly, but other tenses are said of him according to their perfection.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e271.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. The past is said of God by reason of perfection and because he is not new, having been absent from no past time. But sometimes the present signifies perfection better than the past. Things whose being lies in becoming, like motions and successive things, are perfect only when they reach their end, and their perfection is better signified by the past. Things whose being lies in remaining are perfect in what they are, and the past signifies a withdrawal from being. So in God what is signified as a permanent thing ('God is good') is more truly signified by the present, and what is signified by way of act more truly by the past, as Gregory says it is more proper to say the Son is born (natum) than is being born (nasci).
claims: For successive things the past best signifies perfection; for permanent things, the present.
In God, permanent attributes are best signified in the present, acts in the perfect past.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e274.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. In one respect the imperfect past is more properly said of God than the perfect past, since it does not include termination. For what is signified by way of act, the perfect past is truer, since its perfection can be signified only from its terminus. For what is not signified by way of operation, the imperfect past is truer, since its perfection does not depend on a terminus.
claims: The imperfect tense suits God's non-operational being; the perfect tense suits acts, whose perfection lies in their terminus.

ta-l1d8q2-d1e277.summary: Reply to the sixth objection. The future is most removed from divine predication, since it does not yet exist except potentially. Still, it is said of God according to what is perfect in it, namely being furthest from failing, with the imperfection removed.
claims: The future tense is least apt for God but is said of him according to its perfection of non-failing.

ta-l1d8q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 announces three articles on eternity, the measure of divine being: what it is, to whom it belongs, and the use of tensed verbs about the eternal.

ta-l1d8q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 examines Boethius's definition of eternity as 'the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of interminable life'. Thomas explains eternity as being without limits and distinguishes three limits: beginning and end, succession of parts, and reception in a subject. 'Interminable' excludes the first, 'whole and simultaneous' the second, and 'perfect' the third, separating eternity from generable things, from time and motion (even if everlasting), and from the participated being of spiritual creatures. The replies justify definition by negation for simple things and explain the use of 'life' for divine being. Eternity is the measure of divine being though really identical with it, 'whole' and 'perfect' each exclude a distinct imperfection, and 'possession' signifies the repose of divine being rather than extension.
claims: Eternity is being free of three limits: beginning and end, succession, and reception in another.
Boethius's definition is justified clause by clause.

ta-l1d8q2-Dd1e172.summary: Article 2 asks whether eternity belongs to God alone. Thomas holds that eternity belongs properly to God alone, while creatures participate in it partially: hell's fire by endlessness, spiritual creatures by the absence of succession, and the blessed by perfection according to their nature. No creature shares the absence of all limitation. From this he distinguishes time (potency not receiving its whole act at once), aevum (potency receiving its whole act at once), and eternity (being without potency), and calls aevum a participated eternity. Necessary truths are eternal only in the divine mind.
claims: Eternity belongs properly to God alone.
Time, aevum, and eternity are distinguished by the relation of potency to act.
Aevum is a participated eternity.

ta-l1d8q2-Dd1e228.summary: Article 3 asks whether verbs of different tenses can be said of the eternal God. Because our knowledge arises from temporal things, we must use tensed verbs, and these statements are true, since God is absent from no time and contains the perfection of all times. Tensed verbs imply a bodily condition only in their mode of signifying and are therefore proper, not symbolic. The present best signifies permanent attributes ('God is good'), the perfect past best signifies acts ('the Son is born'), the imperfect past suits non-operational being, and the future is least apt but is said according to its perfection.
claims: Tensed statements about God are true, since he contains the perfection of all times.
Each tense fits God according to its perfection: present for permanent attributes, perfect for acts.

ta-l1d8q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 8 treats eternity as the measure of divine being. Article 1 defends Boethius's definition by showing that eternity excludes three limits of being: beginning and end, succession of parts, and limitation by a receiving subject. Article 2 holds that eternity belongs properly to God alone, while creatures participate it partially. From this Thomas distinguishes time, aevum, and eternity by the relation of potency to act, with aevum a participated eternity. Article 3 holds that we must and may speak of the eternal God in tensed verbs. Our knowledge is temporal, God contains the perfection of all times, and each tense fits him according to what is perfect in it.
claims: Eternity is being without beginning, succession, or limitation by a receiver; it belongs properly to God alone.
Time, aevum, and eternity measure, respectively, potency receiving act successively, potency receiving it all at once, and being without potency.
Tensed predicates are truly said of God according to their perfection.
